title: The Indianapolis 500
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on The Indianapolis 500.

hook.text: The Indianapolis Motor Speedway opened in 1909 as a testing ground—not originally as a race venue.

buildup.text: Its first races on a crushed-rock surface were so dangerous that the track was repaved with 3.2 million bricks.

discovery.text: The first Indy 500 in 1911 drew 80,000 spectators and became America's biggest sporting event.

twist.text: Ray Harroun won that race using a rearview mirror—the first one ever mounted on a car.

climax.text: The Indy 500 has run every year since, becoming the most famous single-day race in the world.

punchline.text: A brick yard in Indiana became racing's most sacred ground.

quiz.question: What innovation appeared for the first time at the 1911 Indy 500?

details.summary: The Indianapolis 500 has been held annually since 1911 at the Indianapolis Motor Speedway, a 2.5-mile oval where 33 open-wheel cars compete in one of the world's most iconic and tradition-rich races.
details.whyItMatters: The Indy 500 is one of the Triple Crown of motorsport and draws over 300,000 spectators, making it the largest single-day sporting event in the world by attendance.
takeaways: The first Indy 500 was held on May 30, 1911
The winner traditionally drinks milk in Victory Lane

faq.question: Why do Indy 500 winners drink milk?
faq.answer: The tradition started when Louis Meyer requested buttermilk after winning in 1936. The dairy industry saw a marketing opportunity and the milk tradition has continued at virtually every Indy 500 victory since.

faq.question: Why is Indianapolis called the Brickyard?
faq.answer: The original track surface was laid with 3.2 million bricks in 1909. Though now paved with asphalt, a yard-wide strip of original bricks remains at the start-finish line, and winners kiss the bricks in celebration.
